e.t: This adjective describes something as “inactive; powerless”—unable to act effectively or lacking strength. It refers to a condition of ineffectiveness rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 13:19. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the absence of effective activity or power.

Aendōr, also rendered Aenthor, is a proper name for a place. It functions as a geographical name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: twice in 1 Samuel and once in Psalms. The name appears in the passages as a location designation, but the supplied information does not include the surrounding verse text needed to explain its particular role in each passage.

This adjective means “eternal” or “of ages,” describing what belongs to an age or extends through the ages. It can characterize something enduring, continuing, or associated with an age-long period. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 143 times, so its central sense applies across many settings rather than to one isolated passage. The surrounding wording determines whether the emphasis is on lasting duration or an age-related quality. [p03:word:lxx:L700505:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L700505:occurrences]

Allel, also rendered Allil, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person or family name in the genealogical record of Numbers. The name appears once, at Numbers 26:22. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough information here to explain the person’s role or the significance of the name beyond its use as a personal designation.

Amarias is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times: twice in 2 Chronicles and once in Zephaniah. The name is rendered as “Amarias,” and the available information does not provide a broader common-word meaning or explain the particular role of each person in those passages. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Amisadai is a proper name referring to a person named Amisadai, also rendered “Amisathe.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs five times, all in Numbers, from Numbers 1:12 through Numbers 10:25. The name itself supplies identification; understanding the person’s particular role requires the surrounding verse and passage.

gl: not yet engaged; not yet betrothed
d: not yet engaged; not yet betrothed

e.t: This adjective describes a person who is not yet engaged or betrothed. It identifies someone who has not entered that pledged marital relationship. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus 22:15, so its normal meaning is narrowly represented by this single occurrence. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its legal context, but the central idea is clear: the person has not yet been promised in marriage.

This verb means “waste” or “consume,” describing the using up of something until little or nothing remains. It can refer to resources being spent, provisions being used, or something being consumed completely. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 18 times, so its basic sense is consistent even though the surrounding subject may differ. The precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being consumed and the passage around it.

This word means “merciless.” It describes someone or something showing no mercy, compassion, or pity. Used as an adjective or noun, it can characterize a person or express the quality of ruthless treatment. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 11 times, including passages in Job, Proverbs, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its central sense remains consistent: the absence of merciful concern toward others.

Aoza is a proper name, referring to a specific place or location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Joshua 19:13. Since the available wording identifies the name but does not provide additional context or a stated definition, its dependable meaning is its role as a place-name. The surrounding passage would be needed to explain the location’s role in that verse.

This adjective means “simple,” describing something as straightforward rather than complex or elaborate. It functions as a descriptive word, so its precise force depends on the person or thing it modifies in the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 11:25. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, this entry explains the word’s normal meaning rather than its specific emphasis in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “shake off”: to remove something by shaking it away. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 33:15. The basic idea is the deliberate casting off or clearing away of something that has come upon or attached to someone. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary meaning remains the active removal of something by shaking.

Araas is a proper name referring to a person named Araas. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, Araas occurs once, at 2 Kings 22:14. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the name itself does not provide further information about this person’s identity, role, or significance. Its meaning is therefore best stated simply: Araas is the name of a person mentioned in that passage.

This noun means “number,” referring to a counted quantity or total. It is used when Scripture speaks about counting people, groups, offerings, or other things that can be measured. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 158 times, showing a broad and ordinary use rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being counted, but the central sense remains a number or counted total.

Arran is a personal name, rendered as “Arran.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs 11 times across eight verses, appearing in genealogical material and related family records. Its precise identity and significance in any particular verse depend on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is simply the proper name Arran.

Asarmōth, also rendered Asarmoth, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Genesis 10:26. Since it is a personal name, its meaning is chiefly its identification of that person in the genealogy, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific family context.

This adjective means “disagreeable.” It describes a person or thing that is difficult to accept or pleasing to others. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within Jeremiah 3:7–11. The word’s basic force remains a description of something or someone regarded negatively, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is being described. It is not a name or action word, but a describing word attached to a person, thing, or situation.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Achisamai” or “Akhisame.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 2:32. Because the available material gives only the name and reference, its personal identity and significance must be understood from the surrounding genealogy and passage, not from the name alone. The name itself does not provide a separate common-word definition.

Basani, also rendered Vasani, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs once, in Joshua 13:30. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its specific referent cannot be explained further; its supported meaning is simply the personal or place-name Basani, also known as Vasani.

This verb means “pasture” or “feed”: providing food for animals or leading them where they can graze. It can describe the ordinary care of livestock, as well as animals feeding in a pasture. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 28 times across 25 verses, including passages involving flocks and other creatures. Its central idea is nourishment supplied through grazing or feeding, while the exact sense in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Galemath is a proper name—the name “Galemath”—rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:36. The available lexical information preserves the name but does not identify its referent or provide the verse text. It should therefore be understood simply as a specific designation appearing in that passage, without assigning it an additional meaning not established by the name itself.

Gamala is a proper name, rendered “Gamala.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Joshua 21:18. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, this entry supports the name itself but does not establish whether Gamala refers to a place, person, or another named entity. Its precise reference is therefore determined by the passage in Joshua.

Gelōnitēs, also rendered Yelonitis, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. The word occurs once in this Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Samuel 23:34. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise referent cannot be explained further here; the supported meaning is the proper name itself.

This noun refers to an “office of the,” expressing a recognized position or assigned role. Its wording is incomplete by itself, so the surrounding phrase or sentence identifies whose office is meant. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Psalms and once in Sirach. Without the verse text, its precise reference cannot be expanded beyond this basic sense. It describes an office or position rather than an action, object, or personal name.

Dalaia is a personal name, rendered as “Dalaia” and also associated with “Thalea.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs five times, in genealogical, priestly, and postexilic records. Those occurrences span 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah, but the name itself does not provide enough information to explain each person’s role without the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something fearful or terrible—something that inspires fear, dread, or awe. It can describe a person, event, or power whose presence is deeply alarming. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, including passages from 2 Samuel, Job, Wisdom, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force depends on the noun or situation it describes, but its central sense remains the same: producing fear because of frightening or overwhelming character.

This Greek LXX particle means “in fact.” It adds emphasis to a statement, drawing attention to what is being affirmed or underscored. Rather than naming a person, thing, action, or quality, it helps shape the force of a sentence by stressing its truth or importance. It occurs 278 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its exact emphasis is determined by the surrounding sentence. Its role is commonly that of a small intensifying word supporting the meaning of the larger statement.

This Greek LXX noun means “attendant”: a person who serves, assists, or waits on someone. It describes a supporting role rather than naming a ruler or principal figure. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical text, including several places in Esther, where attendants serve within the royal court. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary sense is someone assigned to assist or attend to another person.

This LXX Greek verb means to give orders or to ordain—that is, to arrange or establish something through authoritative direction. It can describe a person issuing instructions, assigning an arrangement, or formally appointing what is to be done. The word appears 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so its basic sense covers both direct commands and ordered arrangements. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This noun means a “space of two years”—a period lasting two full years. It refers to the length of time itself rather than to a person, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 13:23. Because the verse text is not included here, the word’s exact role in that sentence cannot be described further; its basic meaning remains a two-year span.

The word means “housetop”: the upper part or roof of a house. It is a noun naming a physical place or structure, not an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 26 times across 24 verses, so it is a normal concrete term used in several settings. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and scene.

This LXX adverb describes something as nearest or as a neighbour—someone or something close by. It can identify physical nearness or refer to a nearby person in ordinary relationship language. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing across Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Psalms, and Daniel. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what person or thing is being described as close or nearby.

Ezereel is a proper name, identifying a particular person, place, or other named entity rather than expressing an ordinary action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Judges 6:33. The name itself is rendered “Ezereel,” and the available information does not specify whether the named entity is a person or location. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

“Quite white” is an adjective describing something as fully or distinctly white. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Leviticus 13:24, so this word has a narrow recorded range of use. It functions as a descriptive word, identifying the visible quality or appearance of what it modifies. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the thing being described.

This proper name refers to “Hellas” or “Ellas,” the named place or land identified by that designation. It is not a general description or action word, but a geographical name used in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. The word occurs four times in the LXX corpus, appearing in Isaiah, Ezekiel, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

This adjective describes someone who sets something on fire. It identifies a person by the action of igniting or burning, rather than naming the fire itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a person characterized as one who sets on fire.

This Greek verb means “fortify” or “prevail.” It describes becoming strong, being strengthened, or overcoming resistance. As a verb, it expresses an action or state in which strength enables someone or something to endure or succeed. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 48 times, so it can describe strengthening in a range of situations while retaining this central idea of increased strength or victory. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This LXX adverb means “succession.” It describes something occurring in an ordered series, with one thing following another. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including Exodus, Deuteronomy, and 2 Maccabees. Its basic function is to indicate order or continuation rather than to name a person, object, or action. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word means “smock,” a clothing garment worn over or around the body. It is a noun naming an article of clothing rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 13:18. The word’s basic meaning identifies the garment itself; the surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular use in that passage.

This adjective describes something that is clearly seen, plainly evident, or manifest. It points to what can be recognized openly rather than something hidden or uncertain. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 15:35. The word’s basic force is straightforward: it identifies something made obvious or readily noticeable. Its precise emphasis in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the normal meaning remains clear and visible.

This Greek LXX noun means “acquaintance with,” referring to knowing or being familiar with something. It describes knowledge as a person’s awareness or acquaintance, rather than naming an action. The word occurs 56 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings included in this LXX corpus, showing that it is used across a broad range of discussions about understanding and knowledge. Its exact sense in a particular verse depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as the object of acquaintance.

Etēl, also written Etil, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. Its meaning is therefore its identity as a named term, not an action, quality, or object category. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:59. The available information identifies the name and its grammatical function, but does not provide a broader definition or additional usage pattern. Its precise reference in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the verse text.

This noun refers to the “morning star,” or to “morning” itself—the bright beginning of day. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, so its basic sense is connected with dawn and the appearance of light after night. Depending on the sentence, it can name the heavenly morning light or speak more generally of morning. The surrounding verse determines which sense is intended; the word itself points to dawn’s light.

This Greek LXX noun means “yoke,” a device associated with joining or directing animals and, in ordinary biblical language, something placed upon them. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse. The word appears 64 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages from Genesis, Numbers, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its central idea remains a yoke: an object of restraint, connection, or service rather than an abstract quality.

This Greek LXX noun means “broth,” referring to the liquid part of a cooked meal. It names a prepared food rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Judges, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a nourishing cooking liquid.

Thassi is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it appears once, in 1 Maccabees 2:3. The available wording preserves the name as “Thassi,” but the surrounding verse text is not available here, so no further meaning or description should be assigned to the name itself. Its role is simply to identify the individual named Thassi in that passage.

This adjective means “mortal”: subject to death and belonging to human life rather than immortality. It describes people as finite creatures whose lives are limited. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs nine times, including uses rendered “mortal” in Job, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Wisdom. The word keeps attention on the human condition—frailty, limited life, and dependence on God—without itself stating a particular moral quality or spiritual condition. Its exact force in any verse is determined by the surrounding sentence.

This noun means an immolation or sacrifice—an offering presented through the killing or surrender of something. It commonly refers to sacrificial worship and offerings described in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings. The word appears 367 times in the Greek LXX corpus, especially in Numbers and Leviticus, where sacrifices are frequently addressed. Its central idea is not merely a gift, but an offering devoted to God through sacrificial presentation.

Iamouni, also written Iamuni, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or group in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX, at Numbers 26:17. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise identity and significance cannot be explained further; the lexical information establishes the name itself, not the role it plays in that passage.

Priesthood refers to the collective priestly office and the people who serve in that role. As a noun in the Greek Old Testament, it names priestly service as an established responsibility before God, rather than describing one individual priest. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, with uses especially in Exodus, Numbers, and Nehemiah. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

It means “equally,” describing an action, condition, or comparison as being the same in degree, measure, or standing. As an adverb, it modifies what is said or done rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs nine times; its basic sense remains consistent, while the surrounding sentence determines what is being compared in each passage.

This verb means “treat despitefully; insult.” It describes acting toward someone with contempt, dishonor, or deliberate verbal or personal offense. The word presents insulting treatment as an action directed against another person, rather than merely an inward feeling of disrespect. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, across Proverbs, Jeremiah, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and the person being treated, but its central idea remains deliberate mistreatment that dishonors someone.

Mischief refers to conduct that causes trouble, harm, or disruption. As a noun, it names the harmful act or quality rather than describing the person who does it. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs six times, including once in Esther and five times in the Deuterocanonical books. Its central sense remains focused on wrongful or troublesome behavior, while the surrounding passage determines the particular situation being described.

This word means “tyranny”: rule or power exercised in a harsh, oppressive way over others. It functions as a noun or adjective, so it can name tyranny itself or describe something characterized by it. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs five times, from Exodus through Amos. Its references include Exodus 6:7, Jeremiah 6:6, Ezekiel 22:12 and 45:9, and Amos 3:9. The surrounding verse determines its precise force.

This noun means “long robe,” referring to a substantial garment worn as clothing. It names the garment itself rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 61:3. The word’s precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its broader description, but its ordinary lexical sense is a long robe. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation’s wording rather than merged with a separate New Testament Greek entity.

This verb means “build on”: to construct something upon an existing foundation or base. It describes an action of adding structure where something already stands, rather than simply beginning construction from nothing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 36:43. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the act of building upon something already established.

This noun means “weeping,” referring to the act or condition of shedding tears and expressing sorrow. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times, all in five Old Testament verses. Its use can describe weeping as an outward expression associated with grief or distress, while the surrounding passage determines the particular cause and significance. The word therefore points to visible mourning rather than naming a specific person, event, or teaching by itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “defile.” It describes the action of making something unclean or polluted, whether referring to a person, object, or sacred setting. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person or thing. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 7:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the object being described.

This Greek LXX noun means “side of the forehead,” referring to the area at the temple or beside the brow. It names a specific part of the head rather than describing a feeling, action, or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, with uses in Judges and Psalms. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary meaning remains the anatomical side of the forehead.

This noun refers to pregnancy or childbearing—the condition or process of carrying and bearing a child. It names this bodily experience rather than an action performed at a particular moment. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 4 Maccabees, at 15:6 and 16:7. Those references identify where the word appears, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific use there. Its basic meaning remains pregnancy or childbearing.

This Greek LXX noun means “part intended for grasping; handle”—the part of an object made to be held or used for grasping. It names a physical part rather than an action, person, or quality. The word occurs 21 times in the LXX corpus, appearing throughout Old Testament books and once in the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise role in a particular passage depends on what object or situation surrounds it, but its basic sense remains a handle or other grasping part.

This noun refers to lying down, especially the lying down associated with childbirth. It can therefore describe a woman’s position or condition while giving birth, rather than an action of movement in general. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in the Epistle of Jeremiah, so its precise force there must be read from the surrounding verse and passage.

This word is the proper name “Lykia,” also rendered “Likia.” It identifies a named place or region rather than describing a quality, action, or person in general. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:23. The word’s precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and historical setting, but its basic lexical function is simply to name Lykia.

Maachōs, also written Maakhos, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:40, identifying a named person or place in the biblical record. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific referent must be determined from that passage. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal or place name Maachōs.

Longevity means a long duration of life, especially the condition of living for many years. As a noun, it names extended lifetime rather than an action or a person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Baruch 3:14. The word’s basic sense is therefore focused and clear: length of life or continued living over time. Its precise emphasis in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Manaem, also rendered Manem, is a proper name referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs eight times, all in 2 Kings 15, where it identifies the same named figure throughout that passage. The two English forms reflect alternate renderings of the name, not different meanings. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding account, but the word itself functions simply as a personal name.

Meamin is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:25, and its meaning is preserved as the personal name “Meamin.” Because the available passage information does not include the verse text or surrounding context, the name’s particular role in that verse cannot be explained here. It should therefore be understood simply as the name of an individual mentioned in the Ezra record.

This noun means “sheepskin,” referring to a sheep’s skin as a tangible object. It is a concrete name rather than a word for an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX, it occurs five times across five verses in 1 Kings and 2 Kings. The basic meaning is clear, while the precise significance of the sheepskin in any particular verse depends on that passage’s wording and context.

This word means “eight,” the number that comes after seven. It functions as a number in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, identifying a quantity of people, objects, or time as determined by its sentence. The word occurs 71 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus, showing regular use for counting rather than expressing an abstract idea. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on what is being counted and the surrounding context.

“Autumn fruit” refers to fruit associated with the harvest season, especially produce gathered as summer gives way to winter. This Greek LXX noun names fruit in a straightforward, concrete sense rather than describing a person or action. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, all in Jeremiah, where English translations render it with forms of fruit. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the word’s particular use in each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “dance”: to move the body rhythmically, often as an expression of joy or celebration. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX corpus, including passages associated with David’s rejoicing and with the ordinary rhythm of life. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the physical act of dancing.

This noun means “rations”—a measured supply of food or provisions provided for someone’s needs. It refers to what is allotted as sustenance rather than to the person receiving it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs twice, both in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation, but its central idea remains a supplied portion intended to sustain someone.

This word means “all-wise,” describing someone characterized by complete or comprehensive wisdom. As an adjective, it can describe a person or being as possessing wisdom to the fullest extent; as a noun, it can refer to such a wise one. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. The word therefore presents wisdom as whole, exceptional, and lacking nothing, rather than merely describing someone who is ordinarily wise. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument.

This noun refers to “coasting” or an “aimless voyage”—travel by sea that follows a coastline or proceeds without a clear destination. It describes the kind of journey rather than a person who makes it. In the Greek LXX, the word occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning concerns sea travel marked either by coastal movement or lack of direction.

This Greek LXX verb means “here” or “present,” describing someone or something as being in a particular place or situation. It can state that a person is present, or point to something that is available or at hand. The word occurs 54 times in the Greek LXX, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used in a range of settings rather than one specialized situation. Its exact force in a verse depends on what or who is being described as present.

This verb means “pass by”—to move past a person, place, or point rather than remain there. It describes movement through or beyond something. In this Greek corpus, it occurs six times, including five times in Wisdom and once in Ezekiel. Its basic sense remains focused on passing along or moving beyond, while the surrounding sentence determines what or whom the action involves.

This Greek LXX verb means “tear off”: to pull or rip something away from what it is attached to. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or condition. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 4:38. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, its exact object and force in that sentence must be understood from the context. Its central idea remains the forceful removal or separation of something by tearing.

This Greek LXX noun means “grass” or “herb,” referring to vegetation that grows from the ground. It names plant life in a simple, literal sense rather than expressing an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Malachi. Its exact reference may determine whether the plant is being mentioned as ordinary vegetation or in a comparison, but the basic meaning remains grass or herb.

This verb means “ravage”: to attack a place or people with destructive force, causing serious damage. It describes an act of devastation rather than ordinary movement or change. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. The precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding wording, since the verse texts are not included here, but its central idea remains destructive attack and ruin.

This adverb describes an action done “in a extraordinary fashion” or “openly.” It tells how something is carried out: not secretly or ordinarily, but in a manner that is plainly visible or notably unusual. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, at Sirach 51:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense concerns the manner in which an action is performed.

Remna is a proper name, preserved in English as “Remna” and also given as “Rhemna,” rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:52. The name itself does not establish what Remna identifies; that must be understood from the surrounding passage and its broader setting, not from the name alone.

Rokom, also rendered Rhokom, is a proper name used to identify a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament. The lexical definition gives the name itself but does not state whether it refers to a person, place, or another named subject. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers 31:8 and Joshua 13:21. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding verse text.
